paragraph: Soon after the necklace splitting problem was originally introduced [ 6], Goldberg and West [ 9] 88 proved that a solution always exists if k= 2. Alon and West [ 3] gave a simpler proof using 89 the Borsuk–Ulam theorem [ 7], and Alon [ 1] generalized the results to k>2. Finally, Alon 90 and Graur [ 2] discovered an efficient approximation algorithm for finding a solution with few 91 cuts. Alon and Graur [ 2] also consider an online variation of the problem. They derive lower 92 and upper bounds on the number of cuts needed when k= 2based on the value of n. They 93 also generalize some of these results to the k>2case. 94 In addition to necklace splitting, other fair division problems can be extended to dynamic 95 settings. Kash et al. [ 13] study a fair division problem with divisible goods where agents with 96 Leontiefpreferencesarriveovertimeandgoodsmustbeirrevocablyallocated. Benadeetal.[ 5] 97 study the problem of allocating indivisible goods that arrive in an online manner, again with 98 irrevocable decisions. He et al. [ 11] generalize this to a setting where reallocation is allowed 99 but expensive. 100 ICDT 2026

In addition to ensuring fairness, such data-informed hash maps can even be faster than 105 traditional hash maps [ 14,17]. Shahbazi et al. [ 19] use the static necklace splitting problem 106 to design hash maps that satisfy group fairness. However, making dynamic updates to these 107 hash maps is infeasible without a dynamic solution to the necklace splitting problem. 108 For a concrete application, consider the use of fair hash maps to maintain user information 109 on a social network. Whenever new users join the network, their data needs to be efficiently 110 added to the hash map, and when users leave, their data needs to be efficiently removed. 111 As users’ attributes change, their data needs to be efficiently updated (corresponding to 112 relocation of beads in a necklace). 113 Another concrete application involves table joins in data lakes. Consider an organization 114 seeking to share its data with third parties. The data is stored in a data lake and includes 115 sensitive information as primary keys for certain tables. To protect user privacy, the data 116 needs to be hashed, which introduces the risk of hash collision. A fair hashing scheme 117 must be used to ensure any resulting errors when joining on the hashed columns do not 118 disproportionately impact a specific demographic group [ 19]. For this system to be efficient, 119 it needs to be easy to update the hashes as the data changes.

Consider the problem of load-balancing among multiple servers, where tasks need to be 122 completed in a specific order. Each agent corresponds to a server, and each bead color 123 corresponds to a different type of task. We want to spread the load across the servers evenly, 124 but we also want to minimize communication costs [ 12]. This necessitates having as few cuts 125 as possible. 126 If the order of tasks needs to be modified, new tasks need to be added, or existing tasks 127 need to be canceled, we would want to be able to update the computation plan without 128 recreating it from scratch. As a special case, if computation has already begun, we can 129 still perform dynamic updates that don’t affect the already-completed tasks using dynamic 130 necklace splitting.

Another key application is ensuring minority representation in bucketization. For example, 133 when partitioning data for machine learning tasks, it is crucial that the training data is 134 accurately represented by the test data for reliable results [ 18]. Intentionally designing the 135 bucketization process to maintain fairness helps prevent downstream fairness issues [ 15,16]. 136 Here, each agent represents a bucket, and the color of each bead represents the grouping 137 attribute. If the “red” data is more sparse than the “blue” data, it is important that the 138 relative proportions are preserved to have accurate results. 139

Without loss of generality, assume S[j1]is red. We now construct a more intricate neighbor- 277 hood graph, G′. UnlikeG, this graph is directed and weighted. For each pair of agents A′278 andA′′, there is an edge from A′toA′′if the two agents possess adjacent beads. If any such 279 pair of beads has a red bead on the side of A′, we call the edge good, and its weight is 0; 280 otherwise, we call it bad, and its weight is 1. 281 First, we find a shortest path from A2toA1inG′. Letk′be the number of agents 282 along that path. Then, we move S[j1]to indexj2. Next, for each good edge, we move the 283 corresponding red bead across the adjacent cut. For each subpath of bad edges, we rerun the 284 offline algorithm on the substring corresponding to the subpath. We will henceforth refer to 285 this procedure as ColorPath . 286 Note that the number of edges in G′is at most twice the number of cuts. Finding a 287 shortest path takes O(k)time using Dial’s algorithm [ 8], giving a running time of O(k+k′m/k) 288 forColorPath . Asymptotically, this is the same as Path, but in practice, ColorPath will likely 289 be faster. 290 ▶Proposition 7. ColorPath produces a set of cuts of size at most 2(k−1)and has time 291 complexity O(k+k′m/k).

In this section, we study the complementary dynamic updates of insertion and deletion with 495 two colors. For insertion, we simply give αbeads to each agent and then relocate the αk 496 beads to the desired indices using BatchPath . For deletion, we delete the desired beads and 497 then relocate beads from agents with surpluses to those with deficits, again using BatchPath . 498 Both insertion and deletion take O/parenleftig k′′logk′′ αk+k′m αk2/parenrightig =O/parenleftig logk α+k′m αk2/parenrightig time per bead using 499 this approach. 500 ▶Theorem 17. There is an algorithm for insertion and deletion that produces a set of cuts 501 of size at most 2(k−1)and has time complexity O/parenleftig logk α+k′m αk2/parenrightig . 502 We now show how the running time can be more precisely understood in the special case 503 ofα= 1by bounding the value of k′′askgrows. Suppose each of the beads is associated 504 with a scalar value, such that the position of a bead in the necklace is determined by the 505 rank of its value.6If the bead values are drawn independently from the same distribution D, 506 then the distribution of the rank of a new sample among the existing beads in the necklace 507 is simply the uniform distribution. As such, it is well motivated to consider beads as being 508 inserted into the necklace uniformly at random.
